Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.item: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: This avoidance item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For toxic chemical exposure, the reported triggers, threat beliefs, and memory problems center on unpredictability, loud sounds, incomprehensible chatter, and difficulty verbalising the event. Avoidance of military or police uniforms/weapons implies a different threat context involving armed authority or assault, and there are no corresponding trigger, threat, or memory items linking the trauma to uniforms, weapons, or law-enforcement cues. This creates a clinically implausible mismatch within the five components.

vignette:
Sarah, a 51-year-old married civil servant, presented for therapy six months after a toxic chemical exposure incident at an international government conference. The event itself was one of profound confusion rather than overt violence. A strange, acrid smell filled the hotel ballroom, followed by a chaotic evacuation. Alarms blared as attendees, speaking a dozen different languages, shouted over one another, creating a wall of incomprehensible chatter. In the crush of people, Sarah was jostled and pushed, the feeling of strangers’ hands on her back and arms sending waves of panic through her. She remembers the disorienting arrival of emergency responders in hazmat suits and being herded onto a bus for a mandatory, bewildering physical examination at a makeshift medical tent.

In the weeks that followed, Sarah found she could not adequately convey what had happened. When her husband asked, the narrative would crumble. She’d start to explain the alarm, but then the memory would dissolve into a pure, nonverbal sensation of dread and confusion, leaving her unable to finish the story. This fragmentation of the memory was terrifying in itself; it made her feel that the danger was not truly over but was instead an amorphous, ongoing threat she couldn't grasp or define. This persistent sense of threat made her even less able to deliberately access the memory, as any attempt to do so felt like inviting the danger back in. The memory’s elusive, wordless quality became a trigger itself; the frustration of trying and failing to explain it would leave her feeling agitated and unsafe for hours.

Her life began to constrict around this core of unprocessed fear. The open-plan office where she worked, once a place of collegial bustle, became a minefield. The sound of overlapping conversations, the incomprehensible chatter of colleagues on different phone calls, would send a jolt of panic through her, a direct echo of the conference ballroom. This immediate sense of threat would bring the nonverbal horror of the event rushing back. In response to these triggers, she began avoiding the communal kitchen and staff lounge, eating lunch alone at her desk. She started to rehearse what she would say before any interaction, from a simple phone call to a team meeting, believing that if she could control the conversation, she could prevent any unpredictable turns that might leave her feeling exposed and unsafe. This constant rehearsal made her more sensitive to any unexpected question or comment, paradoxically turning more situations into triggers.

Sarah’s world has now shrunk to her home and, on good days, her specific cubicle at work. She has come to believe these are the only places she can truly be safe. The strategies she developed to manage her anxiety have become rigid rules that now govern her life and amplify her fear. She avoids any physical contact, flinching if her husband reaches for her hand, which has created a painful distance between them. This avoidance reinforces her belief that others are a source of threat. Similarly, her avoidance of medical cues means she has missed her annual physical, certain that a hospital or even a picture of an ambulance will plunge her back into the helplessness she felt in the medical tent.

The feedback loop is now relentless. A trigger, like an unpredictable change to her work schedule, activates a profound sense of threat, which in turn makes the fragmented, sensory memory of the event feel more immediate and vivid. This terrifying memory fragment then compels her to double down on her maladaptive strategies, such as refusing to attend the rescheduled meeting and retreating to the perceived safety of her home. Her heightened sense of threat also makes her hypervigilant, constantly scanning her environment for danger, which makes her far more likely to notice triggers like loud, unexpected sounds or strangers approaching her on the street. It was after she recoiled from her husband’s attempt at a comforting hug, seeing the deep hurt in his eyes, that Sarah realised she was trapped. She came to therapy because she is terrified of losing him and is exhausted by the constant, silent vigilance her life has become. She wants, more than anything, to feel safe in the world again, not just in a single, lonely room.
